description: Family team from Brazil combining science, technology, strategy, and creativity. Rafa (12) loves astronomy and science communication; Luciano brings experience in management, innovation, and AI; Pietro (9) contributes with math, logic, chess, and a passion for games.
summary:
Mars Mission: 30 Sols for the Future is a free educational game for kids aged 7 to 12, built for the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. It runs in any web browser, on desktop or mobile, with nothing to install. Players become Commander Rafa or Commander Pietro of the Naidon family and have 30 sols (Martian days) to prepare a base for 105 people before 100 astronauts arrive.

They choose one of three real landing sites (Arcadia Planitia, Utopia Planitia or Jezero Crater), each with a different difficulty, then manage air, water, food, energy, radiation protection and communication. Every sol brings an unexpected event, a science question and optional minigames (rover, signals, hydroponic farm, shield, oxygen systems).

Space-weather alerts are inspired by real geomagnetic storm records from NASA's DONKI database. The game teaches that space weather, resource limits and teamwork shape life on another planet. It runs in any browser, needs no installation, and is available in Portuguese, English and Spanish. It is an unofficial educational project.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Players run a Mars base for 30 sols. Each sol they plan (build solar panels, reactors, O₂ factories, water extractors and recyclers, greenhouses, habitats, radiation shelters), face a random event with two choices, then see the sol's results and answer a science question. Five indicators (life support, radiation protection, energy, food, communication) show progress toward 100% for 105 residents. A final evaluation and score are shown, with a local Hall of Fame.

LANDING SITES

Arcadia Planitia (easy), Utopia Planitia (medium) and Jezero Crater (hard) change resources, energy, construction costs, events, minigames and the score multiplier. The difficulty ratings are game parameters, not scientific measurements.

LEARNING

Kids learn that Mars has thin air (~0.6% of Earth's pressure), cold, dust storms, radiation and water ice, that oxygen can be made from CO₂ (Perseverance/MOXIE), why recycling water matters, and what space weather is. Bob, a helper robot, explains the game. Minigames: Explorer Rover, Signals from Earth, Martian Farm (hydroponics), Martian Shield (a fictional invention of the game) and Vital System (oxygen).

NASA DATA

Space-weather events are inspired by geomagnetic storm records from NASA's DONKI. The game shows real records from October 2026 (Kp 5.67, 7 and 6) as a "real data" box. When online it tries a live DONKI query; otherwise it uses saved records. These data describe the Sun and Earth; they are NOT a forecast for Mars, and the game says so. Mars facts come from NASA sources listed below.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single file; Canvas 2D for the isometric map, animations and minigames; a deterministic simulation engine tested with automated bots for balance; Playwright for testing. Fonts: Baloo 2 and Nunito (Google Fonts).

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS

Story-driven opening, real landing-site photos as terrain, a family of astronaut characters, a Hall of Fame, and three languages. We considered age 7 to 12, color-plus-icon-plus-word indicators for accessibility, a reduced-motion option, and mobile and desktop layouts.

LIMITS

The leaderboard is stored only in each player's browser. Game numbers (machine output, costs, event effects) are simplified for play. The shield minigame is fictional. Unofficial game, not endorsed by NASA.
